vo: At eight o'clock on a Monday morning, in one of the safest cities in the world…
the police could not even drive out of their own police station.
Their exit was burning. Spikes were spread across the roads. Smoke drifted past the front door.
And a short drive away, in the shadow of a nine-hundred-year-old cathedral, eleven men in black were firing into a single window.
They fired one hundred and thirteen bullets into one window.
This is the story of that window, and of the men who planned for months to break it.
And of what it cost when they finally did: a police officer's life, and Norway's biggest robbery.
Stavanger, on Norway's west coast. A small, quiet city of wooden houses that struck it rich.
Since the 1970s, oil from the North Sea has made it one of the wealthiest places on the planet.
Where there is money, there is cash. And cash has to be counted, sorted and guarded somewhere.
That somewhere was NOKAS, Norway's cash-handling service, with a counting room in an old office block in the city centre.
Behind these walls, millions of kroner were counted, sorted and sealed every single day.
The building sat in the middle of town, by the cathedral, the shops and a busy pedestrian street.
Its security was hiding in plain sight. Nobody would dare to rob a vault in the middle of the city.
The building's real defence wasn't a gun or a guard. It was glass. Armoured, layered, and built to take punishment.
Remember this window. Because one man in Oslo had already decided it was the weakest point in the building.
Five hundred kilometres east, in Oslo, a man was making a plan. He had made plans like it before.
His name was David Toska. Born in Bergen in 1975, he moved to Oslo at the age of ten.
As a teenager he was a talented chess player, in a game you win by thinking several moves ahead.
Before he turned twenty, he was arrested over a robbery where a car was rammed into a shop window.
In 1996, police searched his home in Oslo and found a submachine gun, explosives and a full set of robbery tools.
Police saw him as the planner behind a medicine-depot break-in, a safe-deposit raid and an attack on a postal centre.
In late 2003, a contact told him about the NOKAS building, and what looked like a blind spot in its security.
The money was guarded by a building, and a building can be beaten. The police can always come. Unless they can't.
So the plan had two halves: one team would break into the depot, the other would lock the police in.
He built a crew of former inmates, school friends and new acquaintances, among them Erling Havnå and Metkel Betew.
And Kjell Alrich Schumann, a name that would come to matter more than any other in this story.
Toska moved his family to a house near Stavanger. And here is the part most people don't know.
The fifth of April 2004 was not the first time they came for NOKAS.
Two months earlier, in February, Toska was already inside the courtyard.
He crouched below the window, in the freezing dark, and waited.
Behind the glass, staff were wheeling the money out. Exactly what he had come for.
Through the glass, he watched the money being moved away.
The timing was wrong. He called it off.
He had lain in that courtyard, freezing, for nothing. But he had seen the counting room up close.
In court, Toska would later insist it was never an attempt. Only a plan.
Most crews would have walked away. Toska went back to the drawing board.
And he made one assumption that would cost them dearly: that the window was ordinary glass.

vo: All through the late winter, the gang test-drove their escape route, again and again,
from the city centre out to the woods at Sørmarka, along cycle paths and through underpasses.
Where a car would draw attention, they walked it instead. By April, they knew these streets better than the police did.
At half past three on Monday the fifth of April, the crew was picked up from the house near Stavanger.
Bulletproof vests, helmets, automatic rifles, spike strips and smoke grenades. Everything was accounted for.
It was Easter week, the police were short-staffed, and a warning had named NOKAS as a possible target.
Eight o'clock. Toska's plan gave them eight minutes. Front one: the police station.
A truck is set on fire across the garage exit. Tear gas is thrown at the main entrance. Spikes are laid across the roads.
The truck was full of mattresses and towels from their hideout. Burning them was meant to destroy their DNA.
Instead, it delivered the evidence to the police. Front two: the window.
Toska believed the old courtyard window was ordinary glass. It was not.
First a sledgehammer. Then a battering ram. The glass held.
Toska fired at the window himself. Then he called for Schumann, who emptied magazine after magazine into the pane.
One hundred and thirteen shots. And finally… the glass gives.
Inside, NOKAS employees watched armed men climb into their workplace. Several of them managed to flee.
They are not soldiers. They are people who came to work on a Monday morning.
At least seven robbers poured into the counting room and demanded the money. They got it:
bag after bag of notes, in Norwegian and foreign currencies. Fifty-seven point four million kroner.
At the time, it was the biggest robbery in Norwegian history. And the eight minutes were already gone.
But outside, on the cathedral square, armed men held their positions as the first police officers arrived.
Shots were exchanged across the square. Toska's timeline, minute by minute, was starting to come apart.
Not every police officer in Stavanger was trapped behind that burning truck. Some were already out.
Police lieutenant Arne Sigve Klungland, a husband and father of two, was one of them.
He was in a police command vehicle on Kongsgata, near the Maritime hotel.
And, like the officers on the square, he was heading toward the gunfire.
Seventeen minutes past eight.
He tried to reverse away, but a bus blocked the road. One of the bullets struck him.
He died there, in the middle of his own city, on a Monday morning.
He had grown up in Flekkefjord, and was active in his church at home in Riska. Remember his name.
The robbers loaded the money into their cars and fled the square at nineteen minutes past eight,
along the route they had rehearsed all winter, out of the city to the woods at Sørmarka.
Vehicles were swapped and evidence was burned. Within minutes, the men in black dissolved into the trees.
Toska had planned to beat a window, a police station and a city. He had planned everything except this.
He had not planned to kill a police officer. And from this moment, Norway would not rest until every man was found.
What followed became one of the largest criminal investigations in Norwegian history.
Arrests followed across the country. The mattresses at the police station held their DNA.
That August, The Scream was stolen in Oslo. Some wondered whether it was a distraction.
That has never been proven. But Toska would later play a part in getting the paintings back.
One photo on the board still had no X: David Toska, the man the press called the mastermind.
He hid in Sandnes for days, then drove to Spain. His partner and their young son followed.
He moved between France and Spain, and wrote a diary about the robbery. But he made one mistake.
He kept using the same email address. Investigators traced his logins to Spain.
At their request, the provider slowed his connection to keep him online.
On the fifth of April 2005, Spanish police walked into the Chicoti internet café in Málaga.
The screen went dark.
David Toska was arrested on the spot.
One year to the day after the robbery.
A week later, through his lawyer, Toska admitted planning and taking part in the robbery.
But he denied firing the shots that killed Arne Sigve Klungland. He said he knew who had, and would not say.
On the tenth of March 2006, thirteen men were convicted in Stavanger for the NOKAS robbery.
Together, they were sentenced to a total of one hundred and eighty-one years. Toska received nineteen.
In September 2006, during the appeal at the Gulating Court of Appeal,
after two and a half years of silence, one man finally admitted it.
Kjell Alrich Schumann was the one who fired the shots that killed Arne Sigve Klungland.
And the money? More than fifty-seven million kroner was taken that morning.
More than fifty-one million kroner has never been recovered.
Toska served thirteen years, and was released on parole in 2018.
First, they watched through the glass. Then they broke it.
Behind it was more money than anyone had ever stolen in Norway.
Somewhere out there, fifty-one million kroner is still missing.
And somewhere in Stavanger, a family still remembers the Monday he went to work… and drove toward the gunfire.
